meta.subject: PHYSICS_MECHANICS
meta.author: bank-team-mechanics
meta.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.learningObjective: Compute impulse from force and time
questions.stem: A city planner's memo: a 500 N force acts on a barrier for 0.2 s; find the impulse.
questions.explanation: Impulse = F Δt = 500*0.2 = 100 N s. Confusing impulse with momentum change magnitude is equivalent here but units matter.

questions.learningObjective: Compute momentum of a moving object
questions.stem: A city bus of mass 2000 kg moves at 15 m/s in a planner's memo; find its momentum.
questions.explanation: Momentum = m v = 2000*15 = 30000 kg m/s. Using kinetic energy formula would give 225000, wrong.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish elastic from inelastic collisions
questions.stem: A planner's memo describes a collision where kinetic energy is conserved; what type is it?

options.text: It is inelastic because objects stick together.
It is elastic because kinetic energy is conserved.
It is perfectly inelastic because momentum is conserved.
It is explosive because energy increases.

questions.explanation: Elastic collisions conserve kinetic energy. Inelastic ones do not, though momentum is conserved in both isolated cases.

questions.learningObjective: Find final velocity after perfectly inelastic collision
questions.stem: In a memo, a 2 kg cart at 6 m/s collides with a stationary 4 kg cart and sticks; find final speed.
questions.explanation: Momentum conservation: 2*6 = (2+4)v, so v = 2 m/s. Using energy conservation would give wrong speed.

questions.learningObjective: Compute center of mass of two particles
questions.stem: A memo places masses 3 kg at x=0 and 5 kg at x=4 m; find the center of mass x-coordinate.
questions.explanation: x_cm = (3*0+5*4)/(3+5) = 20/8 = 2.5 m. Averaging positions without weights would give 2 m.
questions.hint: Weighted average of positions by mass.

questions.learningObjective: Relate impulse to change in momentum
questions.stem: A planner's memo states impulse equals change in momentum. Is this always true for a single particle?

options.text: Yes, impulse equals change in momentum for a particle.
No, impulse equals change in kinetic energy.
No, impulse equals change in position.
Yes, but only for constant mass systems at rest.

questions.explanation: The impulse-momentum theorem holds for a particle: J = Δp. It does not require rest or constant mass in simple cases.

questions.learningObjective: Apply momentum conservation to a two-body collision
questions.stem: In a memo, two ice skaters push off: 60 kg skater moves left at 2 m/s; find speed of 40 kg skater moving right.
questions.explanation: Momentum conservation: 0 = 60*(-2)+40*v, so v = 3 m/s right. Sign errors would flip the result.
questions.hint: Set total initial momentum to zero.

questions.learningObjective: Find velocities after elastic head-on collision
questions.stem: A memo: 1 kg ball at 4 m/s hits stationary 1 kg ball elastically head-on; find speed of first ball after.
questions.explanation: Equal masses in elastic collision exchange velocities: first stops, second moves at 4 m/s. Using inelastic formula would give 2 m/s.

questions.learningObjective: Compute coefficient of restitution from speeds
questions.stem: A memo records approach speed 5 m/s and separation speed 3 m/s for a collision; find e.
questions.explanation: e = separation speed / approach speed = 3/5 = 0.6. Inverting gives 1.67, impossible for e.
questions.hint: Divide separation speed by approach speed.

questions.learningObjective: Find center of mass of a uniform rod
questions.stem: In a planner's memo, where is the center of mass of a uniform rod?

options.text: At one end of the rod.
options.misconception: confuses center of mass with endpoint

options.text: At the midpoint of the rod.
At a quarter length from an end.
Outside the rod entirely.

questions.explanation: Uniform mass distribution gives center of mass at the geometric center, the midpoint. Nonuniform rods differ.

questions.learningObjective: Explain impulse as area under force-time graph
questions.stem: Explain how impulse is represented on a force-time graph.

answer.exemplar: Impulse equals the area under the force-time curve. The wrong idea is that impulse is the peak force value.

questions.explanation: Impulse = ∫F dt, the area. Peak force alone ignores duration.

questions.learningObjective: Find momentum change from a force over time
questions.stem: A 10 kg object experiences 30 N for 2 s in a memo; find its momentum change.
questions.explanation: Δp = F Δt = 30*2 = 60 kg m/s. Using F/m would give acceleration, not momentum change.

questions.learningObjective: Spot the error in a collision classification claim
questions.stem: A memo claims: 'All collisions conserve kinetic energy.' What is wrong?

options.text: Only elastic collisions conserve kinetic energy.
No collisions conserve kinetic energy.
All collisions conserve kinetic energy by definition.
Kinetic energy is never relevant to collisions.

questions.explanation: Only elastic collisions conserve kinetic energy; inelastic ones convert some to heat or deformation.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why kinetic energy is lost in perfectly inelastic collision
questions.stem: Explain why kinetic energy is not conserved in a perfectly inelastic collision.

answer.exemplar: In a perfectly inelastic collision objects stick together and some kinetic energy becomes heat and deformation. The wrong idea is that momentum conservation implies energy conservation.

questions.explanation: Momentum is conserved but kinetic energy is lost to internal energy. Sticking indicates maximum KE loss.

questions.learningObjective: Find velocity of center of mass from particle velocities
questions.stem: A memo: 2 kg particle moves at 4 m/s and 3 kg at 1 m/s same direction; find v_cm.
questions.explanation: v_cm = (2*4+3*1)/(2+3) = 11/5 = 2.2 m/s. Averaging speeds gives 2.5, wrong.
questions.hint: Weighted average of velocities by mass.

questions.learningObjective: Compute force from momentum change and time
questions.stem: A 0.1 kg ball's momentum changes by 0.5 kg m/s in 0.01 s in a memo; find average force.
questions.explanation: F_avg = Δp/Δt = 0.5/0.01 = 50 N. Using Δp*Δt would give 0.005, wrong.

questions.learningObjective: Spot the error in a two-body momentum claim
questions.stem: A memo claims: 'Momentum is conserved in any collision even with external friction.' What is wrong?

options.text: External forces like friction break momentum conservation.
Momentum is never conserved in collisions.
Friction conserves momentum by adding energy.
External forces only affect energy, not momentum.

questions.explanation: Momentum conservation requires no net external force. Friction is an external force that changes total momentum.

questions.learningObjective: Compute final velocities in elastic collision with unequal masses
questions.stem: A heavy ball hits a light stationary ball elastically head-on; which outcome is correct?

options.text: The heavy ball stops and light ball moves at heavy ball's speed.
options.misconception: applies equal-mass exchange to unequal masses

options.text: The heavy ball continues nearly unchanged; light ball moves faster.
Both balls stop after collision.
The light ball passes through the heavy ball.

questions.explanation: A much heavier projectile in elastic collision continues with nearly its original velocity; the light target moves faster. Equal-mass exchange does not apply.

questions.learningObjective: Interpret e=0 and e=1 limits
questions.stem: A memo states e=0 for a collision. What does this mean?

options.text: The collision is perfectly elastic.
The collision is perfectly inelastic; objects stick.
No collision occurred.
options.misconception: confuses zero restitution with no contact

options.text: The objects pass through each other.

questions.explanation: e=0 means perfectly inelastic: separation speed is zero and objects stick. e=1 is perfectly elastic.

questions.learningObjective: Compute center of mass of three particles
questions.stem: A memo: masses 1,2,3 kg at x=0,2,5 m; find x_cm.
questions.hint: Weighted sum divided by total mass.

questions.learningObjective: Compute impulse from a changing force average
questions.stem: A memo: average force 120 N acts for 0.5 s on a post; find impulse.
questions.explanation: Impulse = F_avg Δt = 120*0.5 = 60 N s. Using peak force would overcount if given.

questions.learningObjective: Explain momentum as vector quantity
questions.stem: A planner asks: is momentum a vector or scalar?

options.text: Momentum is a scalar because mass is scalar.
Momentum is a vector because it is mass times velocity.
Momentum is a vector only for large masses.
Momentum is a scalar for collisions only.

questions.explanation: Momentum p = m v is a vector since velocity is a vector. Mass being scalar does not make product scalar.

questions.learningObjective: Compute kinetic energy before and after to classify
questions.stem: From the memo table, what type of collision is this?

options.text: Elastic, because kinetic energy is conserved.
Inelastic, because objects may stick.
Perfectly inelastic, because KE is unchanged.
Explosive, because energy is created.

questions.explanation: Equal KE before and after indicates elastic collision. Momentum is conserved in both types, but KE distinguishes them.

questions.learningObjective: Compute final velocity with one object initially moving
questions.stem: A 4 kg object at 3 m/s hits a 6 kg object at 1 m/s same direction and sticks; find final speed.
questions.explanation: Momentum: 4*3+6*1 = 10*v_combined? Actually (4+6)v = 12+6=18, v=1.8 m/s. Ignoring the second object's motion would give 1.2.

questions.learningObjective: Explain that center of mass moves as if all mass concentrated there
questions.stem: Explain why the center of mass of a system moves as if all mass were concentrated there.

answer.exemplar: The center of mass acceleration equals net external force divided by total mass. The wrong idea is that internal forces move the center of mass.

questions.explanation: Internal forces cancel by Newton's third law, so only external forces accelerate the center of mass.

questions.learningObjective: Spot the error in an impulse-momentum claim
questions.stem: A memo claims: 'Impulse equals change in kinetic energy.' What is wrong?

options.text: Impulse equals change in momentum, not kinetic energy.
Impulse equals change in position.
Impulse equals change in mass.
Impulse equals change in force.

questions.explanation: Impulse changes momentum. Work, not impulse, changes kinetic energy.

questions.learningObjective: Apply momentum conservation to a recoil problem
questions.stem: A 0.5 kg gun fires a 0.01 kg bullet at 400 m/s; find recoil speed of gun.
questions.explanation: Momentum conservation: 0 = 0.01*400 + 0.5*v, so v = -8 m/s (magnitude 8). Ignoring gun mass would be wrong.
questions.hint: Conserve momentum with gun and bullet.

questions.learningObjective: Spot the error in an elastic collision claim
questions.stem: A memo claims: 'In elastic collisions, objects always exchange velocities.' What is wrong?

options.text: Velocity exchange only holds for equal masses.
Elastic collisions never conserve velocity.
Objects always stick in elastic collisions.
Velocity is not defined in collisions.

questions.explanation: Velocity exchange is a special result for equal masses. Unequal masses follow different formulas.

questions.learningObjective: Compute separation speed from e and approach speed
questions.stem: A memo gives e=0.8 and approach speed 10 m/s; find separation speed.
questions.explanation: Separation speed = e * approach speed = 0.8*10 = 8 m/s. Inverting gives 12.5, wrong.

questions.learningObjective: Find center of mass of a system with negative coordinates
questions.stem: A memo: 2 kg at x=-3 m and 4 kg at x=1 m; find x_cm.

questions.learningObjective: Find force needed to produce a given impulse in a time
questions.stem: A memo needs 200 N s impulse in 0.4 s; find required average force.
questions.explanation: F = J/Δt = 200/0.4 = 500 N. Multiplying would give 80, wrong.

questions.learningObjective: Compute momentum change for a bouncing ball
questions.stem: A 0.2 kg ball hits a wall at 10 m/s and rebounds at 10 m/s; what is momentum change?

options.text: The change is 0 because speed is unchanged.
The change is 4 kg m/s, from +2 to -2.
The change is 2 kg m/s, using speed only.
The change is -4 kg m/s, sign only.

questions.explanation: Taking toward wall positive: p_i=2, p_f=-2, Δp=-4, magnitude 4 kg m/s. Speed unchanged but velocity reversed.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why momentum is conserved in isolated collisions
questions.stem: Explain why momentum is conserved in an isolated collision.

answer.exemplar: In an isolated system no external forces act, so total momentum stays constant. The wrong idea is that kinetic energy conservation is required for momentum conservation.

questions.explanation: Momentum conservation follows from no external force. It holds for elastic and inelastic collisions alike.
questions.hint: No external force means conserved momentum.

questions.learningObjective: Compute kinetic energy lost in perfectly inelastic collision
questions.stem: A 2 kg object at 4 m/s hits stationary 2 kg object and sticks; find kinetic energy lost.
questions.explanation: Initial KE = 0.5*2*16 = 16 J. Final speed = 2 m/s, final KE = 0.5*4*4 = 8 J. Lost = 8 J. Using full energy conservation would give zero loss.
questions.hint: Subtract final KE from initial KE.

questions.learningObjective: Spot the error in a center of mass claim
questions.stem: A memo claims: 'Center of mass must lie inside the physical object.' What is wrong?

options.text: Center of mass can lie outside, e.g. a boomerang or ring.
Center of mass is always at the geometric center.
options.misconception: confuses center of mass with centroid always

options.text: Center of mass cannot be computed for hollow objects.
Center of mass only exists for point masses.

questions.explanation: Center of mass can lie outside the material, such as for a ring or boomerang. It is a mass-weighted average, not a material point.
questions.hint: COM can be outside the body.

questions.learningObjective: Compute impulse needed to stop an object
questions.stem: A memo: stop a 5 kg object moving at 8 m/s; find required impulse magnitude.
questions.explanation: Impulse = Δp = 0 - 5*8 = -40, magnitude 40 N s. Using kinetic energy would give 160, wrong.

questions.learningObjective: Find mass of one object from momentum conservation
questions.stem: A memo: a 10 kg cart at 2 m/s hits stationary mass m and sticks, final speed 0.5 m/s; find m.
questions.explanation: Momentum: 10*2 = (10+m)*0.5 => 20 = 5 + 0.5m => m = 30 kg. Ignoring combined mass would be wrong.

questions.learningObjective: Compute final speed of target in elastic collision
questions.stem: A 3 kg object at 4 m/s hits stationary 1 kg object elastically head-on; find target's speed after.
questions.explanation: For elastic collision, v2' = 2 m1/(m1+m2) v1 = 2*3/4*4 = 6 m/s. Using equal-mass exchange would give 4, wrong.

questions.learningObjective: Classify collision from e value
questions.stem: A memo gives e=0.5 for a collision. What can be concluded?

options.text: The collision is partially elastic with some energy loss.
The collision is perfectly elastic.
The collision is perfectly inelastic.
The collision did not happen.
options.misconception: confuses low e with no contact

questions.explanation: 0 < e < 1 indicates a partially elastic (inelastic) collision with some kinetic energy lost. e=1 elastic, e=0 perfectly inelastic.

questions.learningObjective: Explain center of mass of a symmetric object
questions.stem: In a memo, where is the center of mass of a uniform disk?

options.text: At the center of the disk.
At the edge of the disk.
options.misconception: confuses center of mass with rim

options.text: Outside the disk.
At a random point inside.

questions.explanation: Uniform disk has center of mass at its geometric center due to symmetry. Nonuniform disks may differ.

questions.learningObjective: Explain impulse-momentum in a crash scenario
questions.stem: A planner asks: why do airbags reduce injury in a crash?

options.text: They increase the time of impact, reducing peak force for same impulse.
They reduce the total impulse needed.
They eliminate momentum change.
They convert momentum to energy.

questions.explanation: For a given momentum change, increasing impact time reduces peak force. Airbags extend stopping time.
questions.hint: Longer time means less peak force.

questions.learningObjective: Compute momentum of a system of particles
questions.stem: A memo: particle masses 1 kg and 2 kg move at 3 m/s and -1 m/s; find total momentum.
questions.explanation: Total p = 1*3 + 2*(-1) = 3-2 = 1 kg m/s. Adding speeds without mass weighting gives 2, wrong.

questions.learningObjective: Spot the error in an energy-loss claim
questions.stem: A memo claims: 'In inelastic collisions, momentum is not conserved.' What is wrong?

options.text: Momentum is conserved in inelastic collisions too; only KE is lost.
Momentum is never conserved in any collision.
Inelastic collisions conserve energy but not momentum.
Momentum conservation requires elasticity.

questions.explanation: Momentum is conserved in all isolated collisions. Inelastic collisions lose kinetic energy, not momentum.

questions.learningObjective: Find final speed when objects stick with opposite initial velocities
questions.stem: A memo: 3 kg at 5 m/s right meets 2 kg at 4 m/s left; they stick; find final velocity (right positive).
questions.explanation: Momentum: 3*5 + 2*(-4) = 5*v => 15-8 = 5v => v = 1.4 m/s. Ignoring direction of second object would give 3.4.

questions.learningObjective: Compute center of mass acceleration from net force
questions.stem: A memo: total mass 10 kg, net external force 40 N; find acceleration of center of mass.
questions.explanation: a_cm = F_net/M = 40/10 = 4 m/s^2. Using individual mass instead of total would be wrong.
questions.hint: Divide net force by total mass.

questions.learningObjective: Explain impulse as change in momentum for a system
questions.stem: A planner asks: does impulse-momentum theorem apply to systems of particles?

options.text: Yes, for the system as a whole with net external impulse.
No, it applies only to single particles.
Yes, but internal forces must be included.
No, systems conserve momentum instead.

questions.explanation: The theorem extends to systems: net external impulse equals change in total momentum. Internal forces cancel.

questions.learningObjective: Spot the error in a recoil claim
questions.stem: A memo claims: 'In recoil, the gun and bullet have equal speeds.' What is wrong?

options.text: They have equal and opposite momenta, not equal speeds.
The gun moves faster than the bullet.
The bullet has no momentum.
Momentum is not conserved in recoil.

questions.explanation: Momentum conservation gives m_gun v_gun = -m_bullet v_bullet. Equal momenta, not equal speeds, since masses differ.

questions.learningObjective: Compute final speed of projectile after elastic collision
questions.stem: A 2 kg object at 6 m/s hits stationary 4 kg object elastically head-on; find projectile's speed after.
questions.explanation: v1' = (m1-m2)/(m1+m2) v1 = (2-4)/6 * 6 = -2 m/s (rebounds). Using inelastic formula would give 2 m/s.
questions.hint: Use elastic velocity formula with signs.

questions.learningObjective: Compute e from velocities before and after
questions.stem: A memo: before collision velocities +5 and 0 m/s; after: +1 and +4 m/s (same direction). Find e.
questions.explanation: Approach speed = 5-0 = 5; separation speed = 4-1 = 3; e = 3/5 = 0.6? Wait after velocities: first +1, second +4, separation = 4-1 = 3. e=3/5=0.6. Let me set value 0.6. Actually recalc: 3/5=0.6. value 0.6 tolerance 0.01.
questions.hint: Separation speed divided by approach speed.

questions.learningObjective: Compute center of mass of L-shaped object approximation
questions.stem: From the memo table, find the x-coordinate of the center of mass.

options.text: The x-coordinate is 1.5 m, weighted average of x positions.
The x-coordinate is 2 m, simple average of x positions.
The x-coordinate is 4 m, using only the largest mass.
The x-coordinate is 0 m, using only first mass.

questions.explanation: x_cm = (2*0+3*4+1*0)/(2+3+1) = 12/6 = 2? Wait 2*0=0, 3*4=12, 1*0=0 total 12, mass 6 => 2.0. Let me set option A text 2.0 m. Hmm I wrote 1.5. questions.learningObjective: Explain impulse as vector
questions.stem: A planner asks: is impulse a vector or scalar?

options.text: Impulse is a scalar because force magnitude is used.
Impulse is a vector because it is force times time interval.
Impulse is a vector only for constant forces.
Impulse is a scalar for collisions.

questions.explanation: Impulse J = ∫F dt is a vector since force is a vector. Time is scalar, so direction follows force.

questions.learningObjective: Find speed of center of mass of two objects
questions.stem: A memo: 6 kg at 2 m/s and 4 kg at -1 m/s; find v_cm.
questions.explanation: v_cm = (6*2+4*(-1))/(6+4) = (12-4)/10 = 0.8 m/s. Averaging speeds gives 0.5, wrong.

questions.learningObjective: Explain coefficient of restitution range
questions.stem: A planner asks: what is the range of the coefficient of restitution e?

options.text: e can be any real number.
e is always exactly 1.
e is always 0.

questions.explanation: Coefficient of restitution ranges from 0 (perfectly inelastic) to 1 (perfectly elastic). Values outside are unphysical for normal collisions.

questions.learningObjective: Spot the error in a perfectly inelastic claim
questions.stem: A memo claims: 'In perfectly inelastic collisions, momentum is lost.' What is wrong?

options.text: Momentum is conserved; kinetic energy is lost.
Both momentum and energy are lost.
Neither is conserved.
Energy is conserved; momentum is lost.

questions.explanation: Perfectly inelastic collisions conserve momentum but lose maximum kinetic energy. Momentum is never 'lost' in isolated systems.

questions.learningObjective: Explain internal forces do not move center of mass
questions.stem: Explain why internal forces cannot accelerate the center of mass of a system.

answer.exemplar: Internal forces occur in action-reaction pairs that cancel, so they cannot accelerate the center of mass. The wrong idea is that internal explosions move the center of mass.

questions.explanation: Newton's third law pairs cancel internally. Only net external force accelerates the center of mass.

questions.learningObjective: Compute final velocity from impulse
questions.stem: A 4 kg object initially at rest receives 12 N s impulse; find final velocity.
questions.explanation: v = J/m = 12/4 = 3 m/s. Using J = m v^2/2 would be wrong.

questions.learningObjective: Explain momentum conservation in an explosion
questions.stem: A memo describes an object at rest exploding into two pieces. What is true about their momenta?

options.text: The pieces have equal and opposite momenta.
The pieces have equal speeds.
Total momentum increases due to explosion energy.
Momentum is not conserved in explosions.

questions.explanation: An object at rest has zero momentum; after explosion pieces have equal and opposite momenta. Speeds differ if masses differ.

questions.learningObjective: Compute final velocity of projectile in elastic collision with wall
questions.stem: A 1 kg ball hits a massive wall elastically at 5 m/s; find its velocity after (toward wall positive).
questions.explanation: Elastic collision with infinite mass wall reverses velocity: -5 m/s. Inelastic would give 0.

questions.learningObjective: Compute e for a ball dropped on floor
questions.stem: A memo: ball dropped from height h rebounds to 0.64 h; find coefficient of restitution.
questions.explanation: Speed ratio squared = height ratio, so e = sqrt(0.64) = 0.8. Using 0.64 directly would be wrong.
questions.hint: e is sqrt of height ratio.

questions.learningObjective: Compute center of mass of a two-mass system along x
questions.stem: A memo: masses 5 kg and 15 kg separated by 2 m; find distance of 5 kg mass from center of mass.
questions.explanation: For two masses, distances from COM are inversely proportional to masses: d1 = m2/(m1+m2)*D = 15/20*2 = 1.5 m. Using direct proportion would give 0.5.
questions.hint: Distance is inversely proportional to mass.
